note: Two things New Jersey states plainly. Every report of abuse or neglect in an institutional setting - and it names residential treatment centres specifically - must go to the State Central Registry, and an investigator has to start within 24 hours. And a complaint form sent to a professional board is a government record: the board may be obliged to hand it to anyone who asks for it once the investigation is over.

civil_injury.summary: Two years for personal injury, which covers assault, battery and negligence alike.
civil_injury.quote: Except as otherwise provided by law, every action at law for an injury to the person caused by the wrongful act, neglect or default of any person within this State shall be commenced within two years next after the cause of any such action shall have accrued
civil_injury.note: The one statute covers intentional torts and negligence. False imprisonment is generally treated as an injury to the person under the same two years, but I did not find a separate false imprisonment section. Child sexual abuse has its own rules (2A:14-2a, 2A:61B-1), not covered here.

civil_minor_tolling.summary: Yes. If you were under 18 when you were hurt, the two years do not start until you turn 18, so the deadline is usually your 20th birthday. There is no general extended deadline for physical (non-sexual) child abuse.
civil_minor_tolling.quote: is under the age of 18 years ... at the time the cause of action or right or title accrues, the person may commence the action or make the entry, within the time as limited by those statutes, after reaching majority
civil_minor_tolling.note: The only carve-out is medical malpractice for birth injuries (must be filed before the 13th birthday). New Jersey courts also apply an equitable discovery rule to personal injury claims in some cases.

civil_government_claims.summary: Against the state, a county, a town or another public entity, you must file a notice of claim within 90 days (a judge may allow late notice up to one year for extraordinary circumstances) and sue within two years; a minor can do both after turning 18.
civil_government_claims.quote: The claimant shall be forever barred ... if: a. The claimant failed to file the claim with the public entity within 90 days of accrual of the claim except as otherwise provided in N.J.S.59:8-9; or b. Two years have elapsed since the accrual of the claim
civil_government_claims.note: Same section: 'Nothing in this section shall prohibit a minor ... from commencing an action under this act within the time limitations contained herein, after reaching majority.' Read on Justia's 2025 New Jersey Revised Statutes page (official NJ site search was not reachable for this section).

criminal_child_abuse.summary: For endangering the welfare of a child (which includes a caregiver causing a child physical abuse or neglect): five years after the victim turns 18, or two years after the victim discovers the offense, whichever is later. Other child cruelty charges (a fourth-degree crime) have the general five years from the offense.
criminal_child_abuse.quote: A prosecution for an offense set forth in N.J.S.2C:14-3 or N.J.S.2C:24-4, when the victim at the time of the offense is below the age of 18 years, must be commenced within five years of the victim's attaining the age of 18 or within two years of the discovery of the offense by the victim
criminal_child_abuse.note: 2C:24-4(a)(2): a person with a legal duty of care or 'who has assumed responsibility for the care of a child who causes the child harm that would make the child an abused or neglected child' commits a second-degree crime - this fits program staff. 9:6-3 cruelty/neglect is a fourth-degree crime with the general 5-years-from-offense limit (2C:1-6(b)(1)). Text read on Justia's 2025 edition; the same wording appears in the 2024 bill S1988 on pub.njleg.gov.

criminal_felony_assault.summary: Five years from the offense for aggravated assault and other indictable crimes. Simple assault (a disorderly persons offense): one year.
criminal_felony_assault.quote: (1) A prosecution for a crime must be commenced within five years after it is committed; (2) A prosecution for a disorderly persons offense or petty disorderly persons offense must be commenced within one year after it is committed
criminal_felony_assault.note: New Jersey uses 'crimes' (indictable, roughly felonies) and 'disorderly persons offenses' rather than felony/misdemeanor. The limits do not apply to anyone fleeing from justice (2C:1-6(f)).

channels.name: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs, professional boards
channels.what_it_can_do: Houses the Professional Counselor Examiners Committee, the Board of Social Work Examiners, the State Board of Psychological Examiners and the State Board of Marriage and Family Therapy Examiners, and takes complaints against all of them through one portal.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed counselor, social worker, psychologist or marriage and family therapist in New Jersey.
channels.how: File through the Division's board complaint portal, or post the board's form to its Newark address.
channels.mail: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs, 124 Halsey Street, Newark, NJ 07101
channels.note: The Division warns that anything you put on the complaint form may become public. The completed form is a government record, and once any investigation is finished the board may be obliged to release it to anyone who requests it.

channels.name: New Jersey State Central Registry (1-877 NJ ABUSE)
channels.what_it_can_do: The statutory report line for child abuse and neglect. New Jersey requires every report of abuse in an institutional setting - child care centres, schools, foster homes and residential treatment centres - to come here, and the Division of Child Protection and Permanency must start investigating within 24 hours.
channels.who_to_report: A child at a New Jersey program. You do not need proof, and you can report anonymously.
channels.how: Call the 24-hour line. If the child is in immediate danger, call 911 as well.
channels.phone_note: 1-877-NJ-ABUSE. 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

channels.name: Disability Rights New Jersey
channels.what_it_can_do: New Jersey's Protection and Advocacy agency, with federal authority to investigate abuse and neglect of people with disabilities in facilities, a right of access to them, and free legal advocacy. It publishes its own guide to reporting abuse or neglect in New Jersey.
channels.who_to_report: A New Jersey program where the young person has a disability or a mental health diagnosis.
channels.how: Contact the intake line, or start from its reporting guide.

channels.name: New Jersey DCF Office of Licensing
channels.what_it_can_do: The Department of Children and Families' licensing and regulatory authority for youth and residential programs, children's group homes, resource family homes and adoption agencies. It inspects them and investigates health and safety violations.
channels.who_to_report: A licensed New Jersey youth or residential program. Allegations of abuse go to the State Central Registry instead.
channels.how: Call the licensing complaint line or file online. Complaints may be made anonymously.
channels.note: Inspection and violation reports, and a summary of any complaint made against a licensed centre, have to be made available on request.
